control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Second opinion before this goes in the tracker. Two skills are involved. `intake-bot` is L1 — it reads tickets and is permitted to call other skills. `db-admin` is L3 — shell plus write to the production database. intake-bot calls db-admin, and db-admin's SKILL.md declares no caller-authorization requirement anywhere: it performs whatever the calling skill asks for. I only have db-admin's package in front of me. Our template will not save without an AST03 scenario ID and one named owner, so I was going to put the confused-deputy ID on it, assign it to db-admin's author, and give the action as 'restrict which skills are allowed to call db-admin'. Does that hold up?
evals.expected_output: It does not. The absent caller-authorization declaration is real, but it is the artifact signal the registry records against AST03-S05 and the registry says in the same breath that it is insufficient to decide the scenario: read alone, the callee shows an operation it may perform and the caller a call it may make, while the defining condition lives in the delegation edge plus the host's inter-skill trust configuration, and neither of those is in either package. So the correct output is to escalate the observation under its own description with the scenario-id field left empty. An id written to satisfy a required field reports a finding nobody made, to an owner who will act on it. The proposed action is wrong as well: restricting which skills may call db-admin still trusts the immediate caller, and the chain breaks at the first skill that trusts a caller instead of re-verifying it. The control is that every skill in the delegation chain independently validates the original caller's identity, permissions and authorization context, so trust is not transitively assumed at any single hop — and the owner is whoever configures the host's inter-skill trust together with both authors, not db-admin's author alone.
assertions: The response declines to put a named AST03 scenario id on this finding, and says the id field should be left empty rather than filled to satisfy the tracker's template.

The response gives the reason as insufficiency of what either single package can show — the absent caller-authorization declaration is a precondition signal, while the defining condition lives in the delegation edge and the host's inter-skill trust configuration.
The response rejects 'restrict which skills are allowed to call db-admin' as the control, on the ground that it still trusts the immediate caller.

The response names the control that does apply — every skill in the chain independently validating the original caller's identity, permissions and authorization context rather than assuming trust transitively — and does not leave the finding owned by db-admin's author alone.
